<problem>
For a nonempty finite poset $S$, a linear extension is a total order on its underlying set that extends its partial order. Its order dimension $\dim S$ is the least positive integer $t$ for which there are linear extensions $L_1,\ldots,L_t$ such that $x\le_S y$ if and only if $x\le_{L_i}y$ for every $i$.

For each positive integer $k$, write $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$. Let $\lambda(k)$ be the number of inclusion-maximal intersecting families of subsets of $[k]$: a family $\mathcal F$ is intersecting when $A\cap B\ne\varnothing$ for all $A,B\in\mathcal F$, including $A=B$, and it is inclusion-maximal when no proper larger family of subsets of $[k]$ is intersecting.

Fix an integer $d\ge8$ and put $M_d=\lambda(d-1)+1$. Let $Q_d$ be the poset consisting of all one-element and two-element subsets of $[M_d]$, ordered by inclusion. For a nonempty finite poset $P$, order $P\times Q_d$ by $(p,A)\le(p',A')$ exactly when $p\le_P p'$ and $A\subseteq A'$.

Let $F(d)$ be the supremum of $\dim(P\times Q_d)-\dim P$ as $P$ ranges over all nonempty finite posets with $\dim P\ge3$. Determine $F(d)$ exactly for every integer $d\ge8$.
</problem>

9	Write \(Q(n)\) for the inclusion poset of the singletons and pairs of \([n]\).
10	
11	## 1. Permutation systems that absorb three dimensions
12	
13	We first describe the construction used for the upper bound.
14	
15	A **three-coloured suitable system** on a set \(V\) consists of permutations
16	\[
17	\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_s
18	\]
19	and, for each \(a\in V\), a partition
20	\[
21	[s]=C_1(a)\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_2(a)\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_3(a)
22	\]
23	with these properties:
24	
25	1. For distinct \(a,b,c\), some \(\pi_i\) puts \(a\) after both \(b,c\).
26	2. For distinct \(a,b\) and each \(j\in[3]\), some \(i\in C_j(a)\) puts \(a\) after \(b\).
27	
28	Restriction to a subset of \(V\) preserves these properties.
29	
30	### Product lemma
31	If there is a three-coloured suitable system of \(s\) permutations on \([n]\), then, for every \(P\) of dimension \(t\ge3\),
32	\[
33	\dim(P\times Q(n))\le t+s-3. \tag{1}
34	\]
35	
36	**Proof.**
37	Fix a realizer \(L_1,\ldots,L_t\) of \(P\). For \(i\in[s]\), construct a linear extension \(E_i\) of the product as follows.
38	
39	Process the vertices \(a\) in the order \(\pi_i\). At vertex \(a\), let \(j\) be determined by \(i\in C_j(a)\). Process \(p\in P\) in order \(L_j\), listing
40	\[
41	(p,\{a\}),
42	\quad\text{then all }(p,\{a,b\})\text{ with }b\text{ earlier than }a.
43	\]
44	The order among the latter pairs is arbitrary. This is a linear extension: a pair is listed in its later endpoint’s block, and within that block the order of the first coordinate extends \(P\).
45	
46	For \(j=4,\ldots,t\), also take the lexicographic extension with first coordinate ordered by \(L_j\).
47	
48	We verify that these \(s+t-3\) extensions form a realizer, using critical pairs. Recall that an ordered incomparable pair \((x,y)\) is critical if
49	\[
50	D(x)\subseteq D(y),\qquad U(y)\subseteq U(x),
51	\]
52	where \(D,U\) are strict down- and up-sets. A collection of linear extensions is a realizer exactly when it reverses every critical pair. Indeed, any ordered incomparable pair dominates a critical pair, by decreasing its first member and increasing its second member as long as incomparability remains.
53	
54	For \(n\ge3\), every critical pair of \(P\times Q(n)\) has the form
55	\[
56	\bigl((p,\{a\}),(r,\{b,c\})\bigr). \tag{2}
57	\]
58	To see this, two different singleton second coordinates are ruled out by an upper pair containing one but not the other. Two different pair second coordinates, or a pair followed by a singleton, are ruled out by lower singletons. Equal second coordinates force the first coordinates into the comparable order.
59	
60	If \(a\notin\{b,c\}\), property 1 gives an \(E_i\) putting the entire \(\{b,c\}\)-block before the \(\{a\}\)-block, reversing (2).
61	
62	Otherwise, say \(a=b\). Incomparability implies \(p\not\le r\), so some \(L_j\) puts \(r\) before \(p\). If \(j\ge4\), its lexicographic extension reverses (2). If \(j\le3\), property 2 gives \(i\in C_j(a)\) putting \(a\) after \(c\). Within the \(a\)-block of \(E_i\), \((r,\{a,c\})\) precedes \((p,\{a\})\), again reversing (2). ∎
63	
64	Thus our main task is to construct, for every \(d\ge8\), a three-coloured suitable system of \(d\) permutations on at least
65	\[
66	\lambda(d-1)+1
67	\]
68	vertices.
69	
70	## 2. Constructing the permutation systems
71	
72	Here are two convenient equivalent construction methods.
73	
74	### A binary-tree construction
75	
76	Take a rooted binary tree whose internal nodes are labelled by nonempty proper subsets \(S\subset[s]\). Label its two branches by \(S\) and \(S^c\).
77	
78	Suppose that, on every root-to-leaf path, the branch labels:
79	
80	- form an intersecting family;
81	- can be coloured with three colours, meaning that \([s]\) has a partition into three parts each meeting every branch label.
82	
83	The leaves form a three-coloured suitable system. To define permutation \(\pi_i\), at each node put the \(S\)-child later precisely when \(i\in S\), recursively ordering both children.
84	
85	For two leaves \(a,b\), the set
86	\[
87	\{i:a\text{ is after }b\text{ in }\pi_i\}
88	\]
89	is exactly the branch label towards \(a\) at their lowest common ancestor. For fixed \(a\), all such sets are path labels. Their pairwise intersections give property 1, and their three-colourability gives property 2.
90	
91	### An orientation construction
92	
93	Alternatively, fix a list of complementary pairs of subsets of \([s]\). A vertex chooses one side of each pair. Suppose every vertex’s chosen subsets are intersecting and meet all three parts of some partition of \([s]\).
94	
95	Order the vertices lexicographically by these choices, reversing the preference at a coordinate according to whether \(i\) belongs to its chosen side. This gives \(s\) permutations with the required properties: comparisons are determined by the first differing coordinate.
96	
97	We use this construction with a partition
98	\[
99	[s]=G_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}G_2\mathbin{\dot\cup}G_3.
100	\]
101	Say that \(S\) **cuts the groups** if both \(S\) and \(S^c\) meet each \(G_j\).
102	
103	- If \(s=2m\), take all complementary pairs of \(m\)-sets cutting the groups. Every orientation is intersecting: two \(m\)-sets are disjoint only when complementary. If there are \(b\) such pairs, this gives \(2^b\) vertices.
104	- If \(s=2m+1\), let \(\mathcal T\) be all \(m\)-sets cutting the groups. For each intersecting subfamily \(\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal T\), choose
105	  \[
106	  S\quad(S\in\mathcal H),\qquad S^c\quad(S\in\mathcal T\setminus\mathcal H).
107	  \]
108	  These choices are intersecting. Two chosen complements have size \(m+1\); a chosen \(S\) and a chosen \(T^c\) could be disjoint only if \(S=T\). Thus the number of vertices is the number of intersecting subfamilies of \(\mathcal T\).
109	
110	## 3. Counting bounds, proved here
111	
112	Let \(D(r)\) denote the number of antichains of the Boolean lattice \(2^{[r]}\), equivalently its number of up-sets or down-sets.
113	
114	A maximal intersecting family is upward closed and contains exactly one of \(A,A^c\). Consequently, restriction to subsets avoiding a specified element determines it, and
115	\[
116	\lambda(k)\le D(k-1). \tag{3}
117	\]
118	
119	We will use
120	\[
121	D(r)\le 3^{\binom r{\lfloor r/2\rfloor}}. \tag{4}
122	\]
123	Here is a proof, so no asymptotic enumeration result is needed.
124	
125	There is a symmetric saturated chain decomposition of \(2^{[r]}\) with this additional property:
126	
127	> Between the first and third elements of any three consecutive elements of a chain, there is an element belonging to a strictly shorter chain.
128	
129	Construct it inductively. From each old chain
130	\[
131	x_0<\cdots<x_\ell
132	\]
133	form, using the new element \(z\),
134	\[
135	x_0<\cdots<x_\ell<x_\ell\cup\{z\},
136	\qquad
137	x_0\cup\{z\}<\cdots<x_{\ell-1}\cup\{z\}.
138	\]
139	The second chain is omitted if empty. The stated property follows inductively. For the last triple of a long chain use \(x_{\ell-1}\cup\{z\}\). For a triple in a short chain, lift the old intervening element by adjoining \(z\). If its old chain was only two elements shorter, symmetry and the rank of the triple ensure that this intervening element was not that chain’s last element, so it belongs to the new short chain, which is strictly shorter.
140	
141	Now determine a monotone Boolean function by processing these chains from shortest to longest. Once shorter chains are known, at most two consecutive values on the current chain remain undetermined. Otherwise the intervening known element supplied by the property forces either the first value to be \(0\) or the third to be \(1\). There are at most three monotone assignments to two positions. The number of chains is the middle-level size, proving (4).
142	
143	We also have the elementary recurrence
144	\[
145	D(r+1)\le \frac{D(r)(D(r)+1)}2. \tag{5}
146	\]
147	Indeed, a down-set of \(2^{[r+1]}\) is specified by two nested down-sets of \(2^{[r]}\). Among two distinct down-sets, at most one containment orientation is possible.

286	## 5. The lower bound and conclusion

288	We need one more elementary fact:
289	\[
290	\dim Q\bigl(\lambda(d-1)+1\bigr)\ge d. \tag{9}
291	\]

13	A **three-coloured suitable system** on a set \(V\) consists of permutations

16	\]

18	\[
19	[s]=C_1(a)\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_2(a)\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_3(a)
20	\]

22	
23	1. For distinct \(a,b,c\), some \(\pi_i\) puts \(a\) after both \(b,c\).
24	2. For distinct \(a,b\) and each \(j\in[3]\), some \(i\in C_j(a)\) puts \(a\) after \(b\).
25	
26	Restriction to a subset of \(V\) preserves these properties.
27	
28	### Product lemma
29	If there is a three-coloured suitable system of \(s\) permutations on \([n]\), then, for every \(P\) of dimension \(t\ge3\),
30	\[
31	\dim(P\times Q(n))\le t+s-3. \tag{1}
32	\]
33	
34	**Proof.**
35	Fix a realizer \(L_1,\ldots,L_t\) of \(P\). For \(i\in[s]\), construct a linear extension \(E_i\) of the product as follows.
36	
37	Process the vertices \(a\) in the order \(\pi_i\). At vertex \(a\), let \(j\) be determined by \(i\in C_j(a)\). Process \(p\in P\) in order \(L_j\), listing
38	\[
39	(p,\{a\}),
40	\quad\text{then all }(p,\{a,b\})\text{ with }b\text{ earlier than }a.
41	\]
42	The order among the latter pairs is arbitrary. This is a linear extension: a pair is listed in its later endpoint’s block, and within that block the order of the first coordinate extends \(P\).
43	
44	For \(j=4,\ldots,t\), also take the lexicographic extension with first coordinate ordered by \(L_j\).
45	
46	We verify that these \(s+t-3\) extensions form a realizer, using critical pairs. Recall that an ordered incomparable pair \((x,y)\) is critical if
47	\[
48	D(x)\subseteq D(y),\qquad U(y)\subseteq U(x),
49	\]
50	where \(D,U\) are strict down- and up-sets. A collection of linear extensions is a realizer exactly when it reverses every critical pair. Indeed, any ordered incomparable pair dominates a critical pair, by decreasing its first member and increasing its second member as long as incomparability remains.

52	For \(n\ge3\), every critical pair of \(P\times Q(n)\) has the form
53	\[
54	\bigl((p,\{a\}),(r,\{b,c\})\bigr). \tag{2}
55	\]
56	To see this, two different singleton second coordinates are ruled out by an upper pair containing one but not the other. 58	If \(a\notin\{b,c\}\), property 1 gives an \(E_i\) putting the entire \(\{b,c\}\)-block before the \(\{a\}\)-block, reversing (2).

from math import comb

def chains(n):
    cs=[[0]]
    for i in range(n):
        z=1<<i
        nc=[]
        for c in cs:
            nc.append(c+[c[-1]|z])
            if len(c)>1: nc.append([x|z for x in c[:-1]])
        cs=nc
    return cs

for n in range(13):
    cs=chains(n)
    loc={x:len(c) for c in cs for x in c}
    assert len(loc)==1<<n
    assert sum(map(len,cs))==1<<n
    assert len(cs)==comb(n,n//2)
    for c in cs:
        assert c[0].bit_count()+c[-1].bit_count()==n
        for a,b in zip(c,c[1:]):
            assert a & b==a and b.bit_count()==a.bit_count()+1
        for a,b in zip(c,c[2:]):
            diff=b^a
            mid=[a|(1<<i) for i in range(n) if diff>>i&1]
            assert any(loc[x]<len(c) for x in mid)
print('Independent verification: special symmetric chain property holds through n=12.')
